title: Chandipura Virus Outbreak Spreads Across Gujarat as Death Toll Reaches 20 With 58 Suspected Cases
excerpt: The deadly sandfly-borne virus, which primarily kills children under 15, has now been reported in districts including Jamnagar, Dwarka, and Panchmahal as health officials scramble to contain the outbreak.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Gujarat reports 58 suspected Chandipura virus cases and 20 deaths, doubling in two days.
  • The virus primarily affects children under 15, with a fatality rate between 28% and 78%.
  • Cases have spread across at least 20 districts, complicating containment efforts.
  • Health officials are spraying insecticides in nearly 500,000 homes and 19,000 schools.

  • Gujarat has reported 58 suspected Chandipura virus cases and 20 deaths, with cases more than doubling in just two days from 26 on July 17 to 58 on July 19.
  • The virus, transmitted by sandflies, primarily affects children under 15 and carries a case fatality rate between 28% and 78%, with death often occurring within 24–48 hours of symptom onset.
  • Cases have been reported across at least 20 districts including Sabarkantha, Panchmahal, Jamnagar, Rajkot, Aravalli, and Gandhinagar.
  • Health officials have launched insecticide spraying in nearly 500,000 homes and 19,000 schools as containment measures intensify.

Outbreak Accelerating

The Chandipura virus outbreak in Gujarat continues to escalate rapidly. From 26 suspected cases reported on July 17, the number has more than doubled to 58, with five additional children dying to bring the total death toll to 20. The virus, first discovered in 1965 at the National Institute of Virology in Pune, has re-emerged as a serious public health threat in the state.

The most cases have been reported from Sabarkantha district with eight, followed by Panchmahal with seven, and Jamnagar with five. Cases have spread across at least 20 districts, including Aravalli, Mahisagar, Kheda, Mehsana, Rajkot, Surendranagar, Gandhinagar, Morbi, Chhotaudepur, Dahod, Vadodara, Narmada, Banaskantha, and Bhavnagar. The geographic spread underscores the difficulty of containing an outbreak driven by sandfly vectors across a large state.

Gujarat’s Health Minister Praful Panseriya confirmed that three children have tested positive for the virus and died, including two in Godhra and one from Rajasthan who died while undergoing treatment in Himmatnagar. Test results for nine additional deaths with consistent symptoms are pending from laboratories in Gandhinagar.

A Deadly Virus Targeting Children

Chandipura virus belongs to the Rhabdoviridae family and is transmitted primarily through phlebotomine sandflies, where the virus resides in the salivary gland and is transferred to humans during bites. The infection is notorious for its severe impact on the nervous system, beginning with high fever, intense headaches, and muscle pain before progressing to altered consciousness, seizures, and in severe cases, coma and death.

“Death generally occurs within 24–48 hours after the appearance of clinical symptoms.”

— National Institute of Virology, Pune

The case fatality rate ranges between 28 percent and 78 percent, making early detection essential. The major epidemic due to Chandipura virus infection occurred in 2003, when over 300 children died in Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh. Since then, cases had been sporadic until the current resurgence.

All confirmed positive samples in the current outbreak belong to children aged 1 to 15 years. There are currently no specific antiviral treatments or vaccines available — only supportive care can improve outcomes.

Containment Measures

Health officials have launched extensive vector control operations across the state. Insecticide dusting and spraying has been carried out in nearly 500,000 homes, over 19,000 schools, and more than 21,000 Anganwadis. Malathion fogging has been implemented in approximately 496,676 households and 19,862 schools to reduce sandfly and mosquito populations.

Health teams from district and cooperative medical colleges, district hospitals, and other healthcare institutions are monitoring the situation across the state. The National Institute of Virology in Pune serves as the central referral laboratory for testing, having received samples from 70 cases of encephalitis. Of the 19 samples tested so far, seven have returned positive for Chandipura virus.

What NRIs Should Know

For Indians abroad with family in Gujarat, the outbreak warrants attention particularly for households with young children. The virus’s seasonal pattern — outbreaks typically occur between May and September during the monsoon — means the risk window extends for several more weeks. Preventive measures focus on reducing sandfly exposure: using insect repellent, sleeping under treated bed nets, and ensuring homes are sprayed against vectors. Any child presenting with sudden high fever and neurological symptoms in affected districts should receive immediate medical attention.
